title: Reservoir-sampling token batcher (exploratory)
content:
Purpose:

This note explores using reservoir sampling as the core scheduling primitive for a continuous token-level batcher. The idea: maintain a bounded-size reservoir of tokens (from live requests) where admission probability is proportional to an adjustable weight (latency urgency, user priority, request age, and KV-affinity). On each inference step the reservoir is drained to form an execution batch that satisfies kernel-friendly size constraints. This approach is aimed at: fairness across short/long requests, controlled tail-latency, and graceful interaction with KV cache locality and kernel selection heuristics.

Motivation / What we are solving:
- Current token-level continuous batchers either prioritize request-level FIFO (favours short requests) or naive token fairness (can starve small requests when many long ones present).
- We need an admission scheme that: (a) keeps long sequences progressing without blocking short ones, (b) produces batches that match kernel-optimized widths (power-of-two/quantized multiples), and (c) respects KV cache affinity (co-locate tokens from same conversation to amortize KV miss/hotness).

Design idea (high level):
- Maintain a global reservoir R with capacity C tokens. Each incoming request contributes tokens to the reservoir as they arrive (up to some per-request cap).
- Each token has a sampled priority score s = f(base_priority, age, kv_affinity_bonus, client_weight). We use weighted reservoir sampling (Efraimidis-Spirakis) to probabilistically retain tokens proportional to score.
- On scheduling tick (continuous loop, or when any GPU is free), we extract up to B tokens from R to assemble a kernel batch. Extraction uses two phases: affinity-cohort pull (try to include tokens from same KV-cohort until kernel ideal width) then fill with highest-score tokens to meet kernel sizing.

Why reservoir sampling?
- Bounded memory: we never let the token queue blow up under spikes.
- Probabilistic fairness: high-weight tokens have higher chance but low-weight tokens still have non-zero chance to appear (reduces deterministic starvation).
- Naturally supports dynamic weights: we can change f(...) online (for experiments) without reorganizing full queues.

Core components and fields:
- Reservoir R: capacity C tokens (C ~ 4x kernel_max_width).
- Token record: {request_id, token_idx, ttl_bucket, kv_cohort_id, base_priority, sampled_key}. Stored compactly; each token is O(24–48 bytes) in the reservoir.
- Weight function f(): customizable, includes terms: base_priority (client tier), age_decay (exponential or linear), kv_affinity (cohort hotness bonus), outstanding_tokens_penalty (to avoid monopolization).
- Kernel selection hook: negotiates desired kernel_width W and quantization q (q = 8,16,32). Reservoir drain tries to return exactly q-aligned widths.

Admission algorithm (weighted reservoir sampling):
- For an incoming token with weight w > 0, draw u = Uniform(0,1) and compute key = u^{1/w} (Efraimidis-Spirakis technique). Insert token with key into R; if |R| > C drop lowest-key token.
- Implementation note: use log-space to avoid u^{1/w} underflow: key = log(u)/w. Keep min-heap (by key) for O(log C) insert/delete.

Batch extraction algorithm (reservoir drain):
- Trigger: GPU ready OR periodic small interval (e.g., 1ms).
- Step 1: attempt cohort-first fill. Pick top N cohort candidates in R grouped by kv_cohort_id where including the cohort will increase cache hit probability. For each cohort, compute how many tokens we can take without exceeding W and without violating request prefix order (must not take token i if i-1 not yet served).
- Step 2: fill remainder with highest-key tokens across cohorts, but enforce per-request token stride (so we avoid taking multiple distant tokens that induce large KV misses).
- Step 3: if final width not kernel-friendly, perform small adjustments: either pad with no-op tokens (when supported) or defer the batch for up to D ms to wait for more tokens.

Token ordering and prefix constraints:
- We enforce per-request prefix fairness: you cannot schedule token k of request R if token k-1 has not been scheduled (except for short-circuiting requests where partial prefix was dropped for timeouts). This is essential for KV cache correctness and for user-visible ordering.

Fairness policy knobs (examples):
- client_weight: premium customers get multiplier >1.
- age_boost(t) = 1 + alpha * min(t / T_boost, 1). Prevents indefinite starvation.
- outstanding_penalty = 1 / (1 + beta * outstanding_tokens_by_request). Limits large requests hogging reservoir.
- cohort_bonus = gamma * cohort_hot_score (hotness from recent KV hits).

Interaction with KV cache and kernel selection:
- Cohort-first strategy aims to increase KV hits: if we schedule two tokens belonging to same conversation after a short interval, the KV cache has higher chance to hit, reducing memory loads.
- Kernel selector provides desired W and quantization q. The drain will try to return multiples of q, optionally by delaying extraction up to D ms. We parameterize D per SLO class.

Open tradeoffs and risks:
- Probabilistic guarantees: reservoir sampling gives expected fairness but the realized per-request tail can vary. Need to quantify variance for SLOs.
- Complexity vs performance: maintaining heap and cohort statistics in the hot path may add overhead at high QPS. Need microbenchmarks.
- Prefix constraints reduce sample efficiency: dropping or blocking tokens due to missing prefixes reduces utilization; we need backpressure/early admit heuristics.
- Kernel underfill vs latency: waiting to reach kernel width reduces latency but improves throughput and cost. Need SLO-dependent policies.

Experiment plan:
1) Synthetic replay experiments (trace-driven): replay 3 workload mixes (webchat-short, long-streams, mixed) with 3 reservoir capacities (C={256,1024,4096}) and measure: latency P50/P95/P99 per request length, throughput (tokens/s), kernel utilization, KV hit-rate, fairness metric (max slowdown factor compared to dedicated FIFO).
2) Microbench: measure latency of admission (heap ops) and drain path at 200k reqs/s simulated to evaluate CPU overhead.
3) Shadow-run on a small fleet: enable reservoir sampler for 10% of hosts and compare production metrics (cost/tokens, tail latency).
4) A/B test on dedicated capacity for premium customers with client_weight=2 vs baseline.

Metrics and success criteria:
- Tail latency (P99) for short requests should not degrade >10% vs baseline under mixed load.
- KV hit-rate increase >= 5% on mixed workloads (goal).
- Kernel utilization (fraction of tokens executed in close-to-ideal widths) improves >= 10%.
- CPU overhead for admission/drain < 5% of runtime host CPU under target QPS.

Implementation notes / Ops surface:
- Persist only minimal token descriptors in the reservoir; avoid copying request payloads.
- Provide diagnostics: reservoir occupancy time-series, cohort distributions, per-request admission events (sampled), and drop reasons.
- Feature flags: dynamic C, alpha/beta/gamma knobs, and option to disable cohort-first behavior.
- Safety: if heap ops become slow, fallback to simpler FIFO fallback queue.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Best choice of key function for continuous weight updates (we currently recompute keys only on admission). If weight changes while a token is in R (age_boost), do we resample? That may be costly. Option: apply age_boost at drain time by computing an adjusted score when selecting from R (but keys would be stale).
- How to handle very long-running streaming requests where outstanding_tokens_by_request is huge? Additional eviction heuristics?
- Does reservoir make sense per-GPU or global across GPUs? Per-GPU is simpler (less coordination) but loses global statistical benefits.

Next steps:
- Implement a standalone simulator for weighted-reservoir admission + cohort drain (Python), run replay experiments.
- Prototype C++ admission heap as a library with metrics hooks.
- Discuss with kernel/runtime owners about acceptable kernel width padding strategies (no-op tokens vs delay).

Appendix: simple pseudocode (admission / drain)

// Admission (per incoming token)
// weight w = f(base, age=0, cohort_hotnessSnapshot, client_weight, outstanding_penalty)
key = log(random()) / w
if reservoir.size < C:
  reservoir.insert(token, key)
else if key > reservoir.min_key:
  reservoir.replace_min(token, key)
else:
  // token dropped, record drop reason

// Drain (on kernel ready)
// prefer cohort-first upto kernel_width W
candidates = select_cohorts(reservoir, W)
batch = fill_from_cohorts(candidates)
if batch.size < W:
  batch += select_top_keys(reservoir, W - batch.size)
if not kernel_aligned(batch.size):
  if wait_allowed:
    sleep(small_delta)
    goto Drain // retry
  else:
    pad_or_dispatch(batch)
